title: Business Funding for Women Entrepreneurs
seo_title: Business Funding for Women Entrepreneurs | Fidelity Funding
meta_description: Funding options for women entrepreneurs: grants vs financing, free SBA resources, SCORE and SBDC help, and how to prepare an application that stands out.
dek: Grants, free counseling and private financing all play a role. Here is how to tell them apart and prepare to use each one well.
intro: Women launch and run businesses in every industry, from salons and bakeries to trucking firms and consulting practices. Searching for funding, though, can feel like wading through lists of grants, pitch competitions, loan programs and private lenders, many of which look similar and promise very different things.

The most useful starting point is clarity about categories. Some money is free but competitive. Some help is free and not money at all. Some financing is private, faster, and costs real dollars. Knowing the difference keeps your time and energy aimed at the right place.
This guide lays out the landscape without hype. It does not promise preferential terms for any group, and it explains where Fidelity Funding fits.

paragraphs: A grant is money you do not repay, usually awarded for a specific purpose and often by a competitive application. Grants can come from nonprofits, corporations, foundations, or government programs, and many have narrow eligibility rules, deadlines and reporting requirements. They are worth pursuing but are rarely a reliable way to fund an urgent need.

Financing is money you repay, whether as a loan, a line of credit, an advance or a lease. It costs something, but it is available on a timeline you can plan around. Many owners use both: a grant for a defined project and financing for ongoing working capital or equipment.
Several resources offer guidance at no cost. Looking into them early can make any application stronger.
bullets: SBA resources, including local district offices and women's business centers that offer counseling and training
SCORE, a nonprofit network of volunteer mentors who review plans and cash flow
Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs), often hosted at universities, for advising and loan-readiness help
Community development financial institutions (CDFIs), mission-driven lenders that serve underserved communities
Local chambers of commerce and industry associations for networking and referrals

paragraphs: SBA-backed loans, microloans through intermediary lenders, and CDFI loans can offer longer terms and lower costs than many private options, but they often take longer and ask for more documentation. The SBA backs loans made by participating lenders rather than lending directly in most cases. Eligibility, rates and timelines differ by program and lender, and you should verify current details on official sources.
If you can wait several weeks and have your paperwork in order, exploring these first is often wise. If you have a time-sensitive need, they may not fit the schedule.

When a supplier discount expires, a big order arrives, or equipment fails, private financing can move faster. Products include short-term loans, lines of credit, equipment financing, invoice factoring and merchant cash advances. Underwriting usually focuses on revenue, bank statements, time in business and credit rather than ownership demographics.

Say you run a catering company and land a $30,000 event contract that requires $9,000 in upfront food and staffing costs. A short-term product could cover those costs within days, with the repayment drawn from the event proceeds. The cost is higher than a bank loan, but missing the contract would cost more. This is a hypothetical example, and terms vary by partner.

sections.h2: Preparing an application that stands out
paragraphs: Whatever the source, preparation helps. Separate business and personal finances with a dedicated account and keep statements clean. Know your numbers: monthly revenue, margins, existing debts and the specific purpose and payback plan for new money. For grants, tell a clear story about impact; for financing, show repayment capacity.

Build business credit over time by paying vendors on schedule and, when appropriate, reporting accounts. Check your personal credit report for errors too, since many funding partners review the owner's profile.

Networking deserves a place in the plan too. Women's business centers, industry groups, local chambers and peer circles often share which lenders and programs treated their members fairly and which ones to avoid. A mentor who has already navigated funding can also help you pressure-test projections before you submit them. Consider keeping a simple tracker of the programs you apply to, their deadlines and what they asked for, so each new application reuses work you have already done.

If you plan to sell to government agencies or large corporations, look into women-owned business certifications, which can open access to certain set-asides or supplier diversity programs. They require documentation and fees or time, and they do not directly provide capital. Contracts won through these channels can, however, create the receivables that other financing, such as invoice factoring, can later support.

Fidelity Funding is a broker that arranges private financing options through its funding partner network, depending on your profile. We do not offer grants or preferential terms based on ownership, and approval and pricing depend on partner underwriting. The initial review uses a soft credit pull, and a funding specialist explains the options in plain English. If you want to see what private financing could look like alongside the free resources above, start the short application.

key_takeaways: Grants are repay-free but competitive and slow; financing costs money but can be planned around.
SBA resources, SCORE, SBDCs and CDFIs offer free guidance or mission-driven lending.
Private financing can move faster when timing matters, with underwriting based on business performance.
Clean books and a clear use of funds strengthen any application.

faq.q: Are there grants specifically for women-owned businesses?
faq.a: Yes, some foundations, corporations and organizations offer grants, but they are competitive, have specific eligibility rules, and are not guaranteed. Treat them as a bonus rather than your only plan, and verify details directly with each program. Terms and availability vary by funding partner and underwriting, and nothing here is a guarantee of approval. Look for programs with published criteria, deadlines and past recipients, and confirm details directly with the organization.

faq.q: Do women get better loan terms?
faq.a: Private funding partners generally underwrite on revenue, credit and time in business, not ownership demographics. Some public and mission-driven programs focus on underserved groups, but eligibility and terms vary. Fidelity Funding does not promise preferential terms. If you are unsure, ask for the details in writing and compare them side by side before deciding. Ask about fees, timelines and whether a program takes ownership or collateral, because terms differ widely across public, nonprofit and private sources.

faq.q: Where can I get free help preparing for funding?
faq.a: SCORE mentors, Small Business Development Centers and SBA women's business centers offer counseling, training and loan-readiness help at little or no cost. They can review your plan, cash flow and documents before you apply. Your specific situation, documents and bank activity will shape what is actually offered to you. Your local women's business center or SBDC can often help you match your business to specific programs for free.

A community development financial institution is a mission-driven lender that serves underserved communities and businesses. Many offer smaller loans and technical assistance. Terms, eligibility and timelines vary by institution, so research the options in your area. A short conversation with a funding specialist can clarify which option realistically fits your profile. Mission-driven lenders may have smaller loan sizes, so ask what range they serve and whether they offer coaching alongside funding.

faq.q: Can I get funding if my business is new?
faq.a: It is harder, and options are narrower. Some private partners require a few months or a year of operating history, while grants and microloan programs may support earlier-stage businesses. A specialist can talk through what is realistic for your stage. Be candid about your timeline, revenue and goals; a specialist can tell you whether private financing, a longer public process, or a combination fits.
